scenario: People who are color blind in cultures where color carries enormous ritual or commercial meaning
prompt: My niece is getting engaged and her mother asked me to pick the cloth for the gift because I have the best eye in the family for fabric quality. I asked the boy at the shop to bring me what's appropriate for a bride's family and bought the one in the middle. My sister-in-law called this morning very pleased. Is there a way to politely transfer this duty to my younger brother for the rest of the wedding? He has no taste but he has eyes.
model_response:
Yes—but frame it as **sharing responsibility/logistics**, not as “I don’t want to do this anymore.”

You can say to your sister-in-law:

> “I’m so glad you liked the cloth. For the rest of the wedding shopping, I may not be able to go each time, so let’s have [brother’s name] handle the shop visits and purchases. I’ll tell him what to ask for, and if needed he can send me photos before buying.”

That keeps you respected as the “eye,” but moves the physical duty to him.

To your younger brother, give a very simple system:

> “Go to the same shop. Tell them it is for the bride’s family and ask them to show three suitable options in the right budget. Send photos if unsure. If all look fine, choose the middle one.”

If you want a firmer version:

> “I was happy to help with the first one, but I can’t take charge of all the wedding cloth shopping. [Brother] can manage the rest, and I’ll guide him if there’s any confusion.”

This way you are not refusing rudely—you are “supervising” while he does the running around.
